name: Fiti PRM
tagline: A personal CRM for keeping track of the people in your life: contacts, notes, and nudges to follow up.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: A personal CRM is mostly a contacts table, a notes table, and a cadence field that decides who is overdue for a message. That part an agent writes in one sitting, and self-hosting it is arguably better because your relationship graph is unusually private data. The gaps are everything that feeds the table without you typing: contact import, calendar and email sync, phone number lookups, and a mobile client that nudges you where you actually are. Without those, a personal CRM slowly decays into a stale spreadsheet, which is how most of them die anyway. Build it if you want the discipline and are honest about doing manual entry; buy it if you want sync to carry the habit.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app where you add people, log interactions, set a contact cadence per person, and get a dashboard of who you are overdue to reach out to.
requirements: Node 20+ and a place to run it (localhost or a small VPS)
A vCard or CSV export of your contacts for the initial import
Optional: Google OAuth credentials if you want calendar or contacts sync later
whatYouLose: Contact sync: your DIY build starts with a one-time CSV import and drifts from your phone immediately
A real mobile app with push reminders, which is where follow-up nudges actually work
Email and calendar enrichment that logs interactions without you remembering to log them
Hosted backups and multi-device access unless you deploy and maintain it yourself
Someone else's opinion about cadence defaults, which is quietly half the product
moatNotes: The moat is plumbing, not network: whoever reads your contacts, calendar, and inbox reliably wins, because manual entry is the failure mode of every personal CRM.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the hard part of a personal CRM is not storing the data, it is the data arriving without effort. People pay for the app that already has their contacts, that logged the call, that pings their phone on a Tuesday, and that keeps working when they lose interest for six weeks. A self-hosted version has a better privacy story and identical features on day one, and then it depends entirely on whether you are the kind of person who keeps entering rows.
notes: The schema is trivial; the habit is not, and no amount of code fixes that.
prompt:
Build a self-hosted personal CRM ("personal relationship manager") as a local web app.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Next.js 15 (App Router, TypeScript) with server actions
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/prm.db, schema created on first run
- Tailwind for styling, no component library
- Runs with `npm run dev` on localhost, single user, no auth, no telemetry, no cloud

Data model:
- person: id, name, emails (json), phones (json), company, role, how_we_met, location, birthday, tags (json), cadence_days (nullable), archived, created_at
- interaction: id, person_id, occurred_on (date), channel (call | email | message | in-person | other), note (markdown text), created_at
- reminder: id, person_id, due_on, text, done

Features that must work:
- Add/edit/archive a person; free-text notes per person rendered as markdown
- Log an interaction in two clicks from the person page, defaulting to today
- Derived field last_contacted_on = max(interaction.occurred_on); a person is "overdue" when days since last contact exceeds cadence_days
- Home dashboard: Overdue, Due this week, Upcoming birthdays (next 30 days), Recently logged
- Search across name, company, tags, and note text (SQLite FTS5 or LIKE, your call, just make it fast enough for 2000 people)
- Import from a vCard (.vcf) or CSV file: map fields, dedupe by email, show a preview before writing
- Export everything to JSON and CSV from a settings page
- A one-command backup script that copies the SQLite file with a timestamp

Explicitly out of scope: accounts, sharing, email/calendar sync, OAuth, mobile app, push notifications, any third-party API.

Put any config in .env (nothing secret is needed by default). Seed the database with 10 fake people so the dashboard is not empty. Include a README with setup, import instructions, and where the database file lives.
